verdicts.rewritten_summary: Guardian/AP (5 Jun 2015): chief judge Frances M Tydingco-Gatewood struck down Guam's same-sex marriage prohibition after an April 2015 lawsuit by Loretta Pangelinan and Kathleen Aguero denied a licence; ruling effective 8am Tuesday 9 June — Guam became the first US territory to recognise same-sex marriage.

Outright country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): Guyana one of five Western-Hemisphere countries still criminalising consensual same-sex conduct — ss.352-354 Criminal Law Act (gross indecency; attempted buggery; buggery with life imprisonment), rarely enforced but fuels stigma. Five of six parties in the 2025 election, incl. ruling party, backed decriminalisation. Cross-dressing law (s.153(1)(xlvii)) struck 2018 (McEwan); no legal gender recognition; 2022 poll: 72% acceptance, 13pp less hostility vs 2013.

Stabroek News (16 Nov 2024): at the IACHR's 191st session (OAS HQ, Washington), a hearing requested by the Guyana Equality Forum — 'Impact of Gender-Based Violence on Migrant Women, Sex Workers, and Transgender Women in Guyana' — heard testimony from Blossom Inc., SASOD and the Guyana Sex Work Coalition; Commission chair Roberta Clarke called on Guyana to take urgent action (record's cited figure: 69 documented cases of violence against trans women 2018-2022).

BBC (26 Mar 2017): trans woman Petronella Trotman stabbed in Georgetown Jan 2017, then told by magistrate Dylon Bess to 'dress like a man' and refused courtroom entry on 2 Mar — case dismissed. Turns on the 1893 Summary Jurisdiction Act cross-dressing offence (124 years old, 'improper purpose' open to magistrate interpretation). Documents both street violence and justice-system failure for trans Guyanese.

Stabroek News (13 Nov 2018): Caribbean Court of Justice allowed the appeal of Quincy McEwan, Angel Clarke, Peaches Fraser et al. and struck s.153(1)(XLVII) of the Summary Jurisdiction (Offences) Act as unconstitutionally vague and contrary to freedom of expression. Backdrop: 2009 arrests of trans women under the 1893 act with three nights' detention; challenge filed 2010 with SASOD — removed the direct anti-cross-dressing offence.

PinkNews (26 Mar 2017): corroborates the Trotman attack (stabbed with scissors/neck wound, glass bottles) and the courtroom exclusion; SASOD's Joel Simpson calls magistrate Bess's conduct a 'dereliction of duty' while arguing Parliament, not courts, must repeal the 1893 law. Unique value: named LGBT-organisation response demanding legislative repeal.
verdicts.note: Overlaps BBC coverage; kept for the SASOD response and distinct sourcing.

verdicts.rewritten_summary: News Room Guyana (16 May 2019): SASOD's Joel Simpson documents police using residual Summary Jurisdiction clauses to extort LGBT people — men in 'compromising positions' threatened with arrest to extract bribes; same-sex couples harassed at seawalls/parks; formal complainants face secondary discrimination at stations and give 'watered down' accounts. Post-CCJ, loitering/vagrancy clauses remain usable against LGBT (mostly sex-worker) populations.

verdicts.rewritten_summary: PinkNews (1 Feb 2019): HK High Court ruled against trans men Henry Tse, Q and R — Judge Thomas Au's 59-page judgment made full confirmation surgery the 'only objectively ascertainable criterion', rejecting self-ID as leading to 'uncertainty and arbitrariness'; the men had already changed legal gender in Britain; counsel called the requirement 'out of proportion'. Current status per freshness: legal gender recognition still requires full sex-reassignment surgery; Sept 2025 LegCo voted the government's registered-partnerships bill down 71-14.
verdicts.note: superseded: LegCo VETOED the government's registered-partnerships bill 71-14 (Sept 2025) after the Sep-2025 court deadline; legal gender recognition still requires full sex reassignment surgery

verdicts.rewritten_summary: HKFP opinion by Nury Vittachi (7 Dec 2016), 'HSBC's rainbow lions: Can we have our homophobia back please?': documents the 2016 backlash to HSBC's rainbow-lion installations — a viral local campaign insisting homophobia is homegrown or foreign-imported, framed satirically. Useful as climate evidence: corporate LGBT visibility provokes organised pushback in Hong Kong.

HK Court of Appeal, Leung TC William Roy v Secretary for Justice (CACV317/2005, Sept 2006): judicial review of Crimes Ordinance provisions setting the age of consent for male-male sex at 21 vs 16 for heterosexual acts — the applicant (21, in same-sex relationships since 16) argued the disparity unjustifiably discriminated; the judgment examines whether facially neutral laws can breach equality. Landmark precedent on equal age of consent in Hong Kong.

Wikipedia 'Transfemicide' (fetched 2026-09-29): general concept article with substantial Honduras content — HRW's El Salvador/Guatemala/Honduras finding that Central American states exclude transgender women from femicide legal frameworks (Guatemalan officials calling them 'not biological women'), and Vicky Hernandez v Honduras at the Inter-American Court as the leading transfemicide case. Background framing for the record's violence claims.

verdicts.rewritten_summary: Croatian legal journal (Igrec, 2026, Elektronicki zbornik radova Veleuilista u Sibeniku 20(1-2):191-206): analyses how police/customs/court officers must conduct searches of trans and gender-nonconforming persons under Croatian law — built on the 2013 legislative amendment allowing gender-marker registration WITHOUT altering sex characteristics, working through the Criminal Procedure Act, Police Powers Act, Customs Act and prison-sentences law with case studies of search difficulties. Documents the post-2013 legal framework in practice.

US State Dept 2021 Human Rights Report, Croatia (SOGI section): minority representatives say anti-discrimination provisions (employment, housing, education, health) are not consistently enforced; NGOs report the judiciary's uneven handling of discrimination cases and limited justice access, with victims reluctant to report for fear of inefficiency and victimisation during trial; hate-crime investigations flagged as inadequate. Official-source evidence on enforcement gaps despite formal protections.

Wikipedia overview: same-sex conduct legal since 1977; life partnerships since 2014 while the 2013 constitutional referendum banned same-sex marriage; full same-sex adoption rights since 2022 (final court ruling); open military service; hate-crime legislation; Pride events incl. Zagreb, Split, Osijek, Karlovac, Pula and the Balkans Trans Inter March; legal gender recognition framework. Reference backbone for the record's dated milestones.

Intrepid Travel country guide: Croatia 'widely accepts' LGBTQIA+ travellers (legal since 1977, partnership/protection laws) — but PDA may draw unwelcome responses in lesser-populated cities and gay venues are 'virtually non-existent outside Zagreb', now improving with new venues in Split, Rijeka, Osijek, Hvar, Rab, Rovinj and Dubrovnik. Visitor-facing nightlife/PDA guidance.

verdicts.rewritten_summary: CroL (May 2014, Croatian): Split got an LGBT Centre (second in Croatia, first in Dalmatia) a month before the 4th Split Pride (7 June 2014), run by association Risp-et; organisers demanded equal treatment of same-sex families (marriage, joint adoption) and said institutions create 'second-class citizens'; mayor Ivo Baldasar attended the press conference. Documents organised community infrastructure on the coast.

CroL (Oct 2014, Croatian): presentation of LGBTIQ+ centre 'Druga Rijeka' in Rijeka — founded to develop the community in Primorsko-goranska county and network with national/international organisations, backed publicly by mayor Vojko Obersnel and cultural institutions; goals include visibility, anti-discrimination work and quality-of-life advocacy. Second major community centre documented.
